title: Hand-scored interpretability, features against neurons
takeaway: A blinded human rater scored features and MLP neurons on the same 0–14 interpretability rubric, and the two score distributions barely overlap: the median neuron scores 0, meaning no hypothesis could be formed at all, while the median feature scores 12. It is the paper's central human-judgment evidence that dictionary learning produces more interpretable units than the neuron basis — resting on one rater and a small sample.
walkthrough:
**What you are looking at.** Two histograms drawn over one pair of axes. The horizontal axis, *Rubric Value*, is a single interpretability score running from 0 to 14. The vertical axis, *Count*, is how many scored units landed at each score, with one bar over each whole number.

Crimson bars are [[feature|features]], the dictionary directions the [[sparse-autoencoder|sparse autoencoder]] learned. Teal bars are ordinary MLP neurons from the same [[one-layer-transformer-testbed|one-layer model]]. Where both colours have a bar at the same score, the shorter one shows through as dark navy — that navy block is overlap, not a third category.

The two coloured boxes at the right give each distribution's median and mean. The small triangles under the axis mark those medians on the scale itself: teal at 0, crimson at 12.

**Where a score comes from.** One author rated every unit [[blinded-annotation|without being told]] whether it was a feature or a neuron. The [[feature-interpretability-rubric|rubric]] (Appendix 14) has the rater commit to an interpretation first, then score the evidence against it: confidence in that interpretation (0–3), how consistent the highest-activating tokens are with it (0–5), how consistent the [[logit-weight|positive logit weights]] are with it (0–3), one point if inconsistent logit effects were at least clearly smaller than the consistent ones ([[rubric-effect-size-separation|an effect-size separation]]), and specificity (0–3). Those ranges sum to 15, but 14 is the stated maximum. A perfect 3 on logit consistency means nothing was inconsistent, so the separation point cannot then be earned.

The rater was not shown only top-activating examples. That is deliberate: a [[polysemanticity|polysemantic]] neuron often looks clean at its maximum and messy further down ([[max-dataset-example-bias|the maximal-example weakness]]). Each unit's range was therefore cut into eleven evenly spaced [[activation-interval|activation intervals]], sampled uniformly.

**What it shows.** The teal distribution piles up at 0. Its remaining mass is thin, spread from 2 to 8 with a few strays as high as 13, for a mean of 3.2.

The crimson distribution sits almost entirely above 8 — the level the authors call "quite interpretable", explicitly as a subjective judgment — and climbs towards the top of the scale.

**How much weight it carries.** The whole comparison rests on 412 interval judgements across 162 units, from a single rater. The paper says outright that the procedure is labour-intensive and the sample is small, and lists further [[interpretability-evaluation-caveats|caveats]] on how the units were sampled.

terms.definition: The chart title. It marks this as the human-judgment arm of the paper's interpretability evaluation, as opposed to the two automated-interpretability arms that follow it.

The horizontal axis: the total interpretability score a unit received, summed over the five scored items of the appendix rubric. Higher means the rater had a more confident, more specific interpretation that the evidence backed up.
The vertical axis: the number of scored units whose rubric value fell in that bar. Each unit contributes to exactly one bar.

The crimson series. A feature here is one hidden unit of the trained sparse autoencoder, equivalently one direction in the learned dictionary, which the paper proposes as a replacement for the neuron as the unit of analysis.
The teal series. These are the 512 ReLU units of the subject transformer's MLP layer, scored on the same rubric as the features so the two can be compared directly.
Reported in each legend box: the middle rubric value of that series. It is quoted alongside the mean because both distributions are lopsided, and the median is the less fragile summary of the two.

Reported in each legend box: the arithmetic average rubric value of that series. For neurons it sits well above the median, which tells you a minority of neurons scored well while the bulk scored zero.
The legend entry for the small triangles beneath the horizontal axis. Each triangle marks its series' median at the corresponding position on the rubric scale.

Not a third series. Where a crimson bar and a teal bar cover the same rubric value, the colours blend, so the navy region is the height of whichever bar is shorter and the pure colour above it belongs to the taller one.
The rater — one of the authors — was not told whether the unit on screen was an autoencoder feature or an MLP neuron. This is what keeps the comparison between the two series from being circular.

One of eleven evenly spaced bands between zero activation and a unit's maximum activation. Examples were drawn from each band so the rater saw the whole activation spectrum, not only the strongest firings.

In the paper's inspection interface, the tokens on which a unit fires strongly are bolded within their surrounding text. Rubric item two asks how consistent those tokens are with the rater's stated interpretation.

A feature's logit weights are how much its firing pushes each next-token logit up or down; the positive ones are the tokens it promotes. Rubric item three asks whether the tokens a unit promotes make sense given the interpretation of when it fires.

A one-point rubric item, awarded when some promoted tokens contradict the interpretation but are clearly weaker than the ones that fit. It is a partial-credit item, so it is unavailable when the logit-consistency item already scored full marks.
The final rubric item, 0–3. It asks how narrow the interpretation is — 'fires on Arabic script' is more specific, and so scores higher, than 'fires on non-English text'.

The first scored rubric item, 0–3: how sure the rater is of the interpretation they formed. A neuron for which no interpretation could be formed at all scores zero here and, in practice, zero overall.

numbers.meaning: The range of the horizontal axis, and the range of the rubric. Zero means the rater could not form any hypothesis about the unit; 14 is the highest total the five items can jointly produce.

The per-item maxima of the rubric: confidence (0–3), consistency of high-activation tokens (0–5), consistency of positive logit effects (0–3), effect-size separation (0 or 1), specificity (0–3). Their nominal sum is 15.

The actual maximum score, one below the nominal 15. Scoring the full 3 for logit consistency means no logit effects were inconsistent, which makes the 1-point separation item inapplicable, so the two cannot both be maxed.
The number of activation intervals scored in total. Each interval is one band of one unit's activation spectrum, examined and judged against that unit's overall interpretation.
The number of units — features and neurons combined — that received a rubric score. The heights of all the bars in this chart add to roughly this figure, so each unit contributes one bar increment.

412 intervals divided by 162 units: on average about two and a half intervals were examined per unit, well short of the eleven a unit can have. The paper does not spell out how intervals were allocated across units.

The number of evenly spaced activation intervals a unit's spectrum is divided into, from zero activation up to its maximum. Sampling uniformly across these is what stops the evaluation from resting on top examples alone.
Half the scored features reached 12 or better. The paper reads a 12 as an interpretation the rater was confident in, that was specific, and that also made sense of the feature's logit weights.
The average feature score. It sits below the median because a small left tail of poorly-scoring features drags it down, while the bulk of the distribution is bunched near the ceiling.
Half the scored neurons received zero. Zero is not 'a weak interpretation' but 'no interpretation was formed', which is the sharpest single number in the figure.

The average neuron score, far above the median of 0. The gap says the non-zero neurons are a minority carrying most of the total, consistent with a few genuinely monosemantic neurons among many polysemantic ones.
The rubric value above which the authors say they subjectively found features to be 'quite interpretable'. It is offered as a rough reading aid for the axis, not as a validated threshold.

Read off the bar heights, roughly this is how the 162 scored units split between the two series; the paper does not state the split. The neuron and feature histograms are therefore not directly comparable in absolute height, only in shape.

numbers.value: Tallest teal bar ≈ 24, at rubric value 0
numbers.meaning: The count of neurons scoring zero. It is about half of all scored neurons, which is why the neuron median lands exactly on 0.

numbers.value: Tallest crimson bars ≈ 23 at 13 and ≈ 20 at 14
numbers.meaning: The peak of the feature distribution sits at the top end of the scale rather than in the middle. Together these two bars hold something like a third of all scored features.
The rising staircase between 9 and 13. Feature counts increase steadily with rubric value across this stretch, which is the shape that distinguishes the crimson series from the teal one.

numbers.value: Feature counts of about 1 each at rubric values 3–6, and about 2 at 0
numbers.meaning: The feature distribution's left tail. A handful of features were as uninterpretable as a typical neuron, so the claim is about the bulk of features, not about every feature.
Both series have an empty bar at 1. A total of exactly 1 would require near-zero on every item while still scoring something, which the rubric makes an unlikely combination.
The count scale, which tops out just above 24 to accommodate the two tallest bars. Bar heights quoted here are read off this scale and are accurate to about one unit.
The width of the subject transformer's MLP, so the number of neurons available to sample from. The model has a 128-dimensional residual stream and a ReLU MLP.

The A/1 autoencoder's learned features, of which 168 are dead (never active over 100 million examples) and 292 are ultralow density (active on fewer than one in a million). Both groups are excluded before features are sampled for scoring, so this chart describes the remaining ~3,636.
